To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in mice, unlike rats, photoreceptor L-Type calcium channel (LTCA) activity in vivo does not increase until after 20 months of age.
the calcium hypothesis of retinal aging in mice is confirmed by a d-cis-diltaizem-insensitive uptake spike in 10-month old mice that is not seen in rats.
the calcium hypothesis of aging in mice is confirmed and that the calcium hypothesis is not confirmed for rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the retinopathy that is responsible for the age-related declines in visual acuity in the rat and mouse.
the development of a personalized approach to photoreceptor aging and its treatment.
the development of a new approach to the development of the calcium hypothesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the calcium hypothesis was confirmed by these data.
the calcium hypothesis was confirmed in the mouse, and the hypothesis was supported in the rat.
the calcium hypothesis was confirmed in mice, but not in rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the calcium hypothesis of aging is not applicable to mice, and that we have identified a new phenomenon in mice, the manganese uptake spike, that is diltiazem-insenstive in the light and diltiazeme-sensitive in the dark.
the calcium hypothesis is supported in mice and that the calcium hypothesis can be personalized for individual animals.
photoreceptor L type Ca2+ channel activity in mice does not increase until after 1 year of age, and this is consistent with stable photopic visual performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the calcium hypothesis to predict the age of onset of age-related declines in visual performance in mice and that we can use d-cis-ditiazem to treat these declines.
the calcium hypothesis of aging is a useful tool for understanding the mechanisms of aging in the retina.
the mouse is an excellent model of normal photoreceptor aging and that photoreceptor L-channel calcium activity in mice does not progressively increase before 18 month of age.
